narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A musicologist or dance historian with a focus on Russian folk traditions.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Kamarinskaya originated as a traditional Russian folk dance and song.
Mikhail Glinka composed his orchestral version in 1848, which premiered in St. Petersburg on March 15, 1850, under the direction of K. N. Albrecht.
on_screen: Map: Russia · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is a traditional folk form; Glinka’s orchestral interpretation uses a bridal song, 'Iz-za gor', as a contrasting theme to the dance melody.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is traditionally performed as a squatting dance, often referred to as a Kazatsky.
It is characterized by a quick, repetitive tune that dictates the dancer's movements, which continue in a perpetual motion fashion.
Watch for Kazatsky squat.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (93UeF2JMxYg)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Traditional accompaniment is provided by a fiddler, a balalaika player, or a concertina player.
The music is defined by three-bar phrase lengths and an ostinato melody.
Listen for the Fiddle, Balalaika, Concertina.
A quick, driving instrumental melody characterized by a three-bar phrase structure that repeats indefinitely, creating a sense of perpetual motion.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Kamarinskaya — Mikhail Glinka
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Three-bar phrase lengths played in moto perpetuo.

The dance is associated with the Kazatsky style, which has been linked in romantic fashion to Cossacks.
It is a type of Russian plyaska (folk dance).

music_brief.purpose: copyright-free soundtrack with the same DNA as the tradition's music — an original creation, not a reproduction
music_brief.rhythm_pattern: Three-bar phrase lengths played in moto perpetuo.
music_brief.sound_description: A quick, driving instrumental melody characterized by a three-bar phrase structure that repeats indefinitely, creating a sense of perpetual motion.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Kamarinskaya (Russia). Rhythm pattern: Three-bar phrase lengths played in moto perpetuo.. Instruments: Fiddle, Balalaika, Concertina. Form: Ostinato-based dance tune.. Mood: Lively, Repetitive, Driving. It should sound like this: A quick, driving instrumental melody characterized by a three-bar phrase structure that repeats indefinitely, creating a sense of perpetual motion. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress: the sources do not describe the costume yet
care: every element traceable to the costume notes or a licensed image; nothing added for effect
no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
a culture bearer reviews the wardrobe before production; the review is recorded in the pack
credits name the tradition and the sources of the reconstruction
